name: Lead cosmetics hair loss and mottled skin

card.summary: The documented skin and hair damage from lead-based white face paint (ceruse), a historical complexion product used to look pale and blemish-free.
card.note: Lead is a toxic metal; the harms described here are historical and still relevant to lead-containing cosmetics.

quick.overview:
Ceruse, a paste of white lead and vinegar, was the prestige complexion product of Renaissance and later Europe. It covered scars and blemishes and gave a pale, opaque finish that signalled wealth.

Its cost to appearance became part of its story: long-term use is described as leaving skin mottled and peeling, and thinning hair, especially at the hairline. Users often layered on more paint to hide the damage, a cycle historians describe as dependence.
quick.how: Historically ceruse was mixed into a paste and applied to the face, neck and chest, with makers varying quality and price; the best Venetian grade was the most expensive. Hairline loss may have coincided with the fashion for high foreheads.
quick.risks: Lead poisoning is associated with skin damage, hair loss, abdominal pain, paralysis, confusion, convulsions, reduced fertility and death. The WHO listed lead among chemicals of concern in cosmetics in 2010.

lead: Lead cosmetics, chiefly white lead ceruse, were used for centuries to give the face a pale, smooth, blemish-concealing finish. The same products are documented as causing hair loss and mottled, peeling skin with long use.[1]

Ceruse was a paste of basic lead carbonate mixed with water and vinegar. It was opaque, covered scars and spots, and had a drying, cooling effect, which is why it sold at a premium, with Venetian ceruse the most prized.[1] Its use peaked in the sixteenth century, when pale skin signalled wealth and freedom from outdoor labour.[1]

Historical accounts describe a cycle: skin damaged by lead was covered with further layers. Hair loss, especially at the hairline, may have contributed to fashions for a high forehead, though syphilis, which also causes hair loss, has been suggested as another cause.[1] Several noted users, such as Maria Gunning, Countess of Coventry, who died at 27 in 1760, are linked in popular accounts to lead poisoning.[1]

angle.text: Ceruse gave an immediate pale, even surface, which is why it was used. The article documents what happened with long use: mottled, peeling skin and hair loss.

paras: Ceruse was made by exposing lead sheets to vinegar in sealed pots for weeks, converting them to lead acetate and then lead carbonate, which was ground and mixed into a paste.[1] Lead-based whitening goes back to ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome, and Italy exported ceruse from the fourteenth century.[1]
Long-term use is described as making the skin mottle and peel, leaving blemishes that users covered with more layers, producing a cycle of reliance.[1]

Lead poisoning is listed among the causes of hair loss in historical accounts of ceruse, with thinning especially at the hairline; some writers connect this with the fashionable high forehead, while syphilis is another possible cause of hair loss in the period.[1]

Other documented effects include abdominal pain, paralysis, confusion, convulsions, reduced fertility, organ damage and death.[1] Scientific studies confirming the severity of lead's effects emerged at the end of the eighteenth century, and in 2010 the WHO listed lead among ten major chemicals of concern in cosmetics.[1] Lead was one of several toxic whiteners, alongside mercury, used in Europe and later the United States.[2]

timeline.event: Maria Gunning, Countess of Coventry, dies aged 27, reportedly from lead poisoning.[1]
WHO lists lead among major chemicals of concern in cosmetics.[1]
